headline: Xiaomi 18 Fold packs 200MP camera, 6,000mAh battery and new Arm GPU, outperforming Samsung's foldable
summary: The 18 Fold features a powerful Xring O3 chip and a triple Leica camera system, aiming to surpass rivals. It's available in China from ¥10,999 (approx. $1,600).
details: Xiaomi has unveiled the 18 Fold, its first book-style foldable since 2024, adopting a short, wide design similar to Huawei and Samsung. It aims to surpass rivals with superior specs, including Xiaomi's new Xring O3 chipset and Arm's Mali G2-Ultra NX GPU.

The phone features a 7.58-inch inner and 5.38-inch outer screen, both with a 1.4:1 aspect ratio, ideal for movies and ebooks. Its compact form factor makes it pocketable when closed, with a comfortable cover screen for single-handed use.

While visually appealing in black, white, red, or a pink ceramic edition, the 18 Fold is slightly heavier and thicker than Samsung's Z Fold 8. Xiaomi has not announced any IP rating, and the crease appears more noticeable than on current Samsung foldables.

Performance is boosted by the Xring O3 chipset, promising Snapdragon 8 Elite-level power. This also marks the debut of Arm's Mali G2-Ultra NX GPU, bringing mobile-first support for DLSS-style graphics acceleration to Android.

The device boasts a substantial 6,000mAh silicon-carbon battery, significantly larger than Samsung's 4,800mAh, with 67W wired and 50W wireless charging. Both OLED displays achieve an impressive peak brightness of 4,000 nits.

Photography is a major focus, with a triple rear camera system developed in partnership with Leica. It includes a 200-megapixel main sensor, a 50-megapixel 3.5x periscope telephoto lens, and a 50-megapixel ultrawide camera.

Reviewers note that by addressing the camera shortcomings of competitors and improving battery and display, Xiaomi has created a strong contender in the foldable market. However, the absence of an IP rating remains a concern.

The Xiaomi 18 Fold is currently available for preorder in China starting from ¥10,999 (approximately $1,600), with official sales beginning September 10th. An international launch has not yet been confirmed by Xiaomi.

headline_marked: [[Intel surpasses one million High-NA EUV wafers processed]], outpaces the rest of the industry combined
headline: Intel surpasses one million High-NA EUV wafers processed, outpaces the rest of the industry combined
summary: Intel has processed over one million 300-mm wafers with High-NA EUV, exceeding the rest of the industry combined. The company is also pioneering larger 6x12-inch photomasks to boost production and cut costs.
details: Intel announced it has processed over one million 300-mm wafers using its High-NA EUV scanners, less than two and a half years after the first tool was assembled. This figure includes wafers from tool installation, R&D, and production, with High-NA EUV now certified for Intel's 18A process technology and used for Panther Lake processors.

This million-wafer milestone signifies Intel's fleet and process maturity, making it the first in the industry to achieve such a feat. Notably, Intel has processed more wafers using High-NA tools than the rest of the industry combined, surpassing the 500,000 wafers total announced by ASML for all other High-NA EUV scanners shipped.

Current 0.55-NA EUV uses anamorphic 4X/8X magnification, meaning standard 6-inch photomasks can only expose 26x16.5 mm half-fields. This necessitates 'stitching' for larger dies that would typically fit a conventional 26x33 mm EUV field, requiring two separate exposures.

Stitching presents several drawbacks, including a significant reduction in throughput from 175 to 125 wafers per hour on an EXE:5200B scanner. It also limits floor planning freedom as chip designs must account for stitching, and precise alignment is critical to avoid defects and reduced yields, especially for large CPU and GPU dies.

To overcome stitching, Intel is leading an industry shift towards larger 6x12-inch photomasks. These larger masks would enable High-NA EUV scanners to expose a full 26x33 mm field in a single pass, eliminating the need for stitching and its associated complexities.

However, transitioning to 6x12-inch photomasks requires substantial changes across the entire mask ecosystem. This includes modifications to mask blanks, deposition, etching, inspection, metrology, cleaning, pellicles, mask writers, and mask handling systems, as well as potential redesigns or modifications to High-NA EUV scanners themselves.

While this represents a major retooling effort for the semiconductor supply chain, Intel appears to be the primary advocate for changing this long-standing mask standard. If successful, Intel could gain a significant first-mover advantage, defining the future standard for projection lithography.
